summary: Follow-up on 2027-02-21 incident where Aurora saw degraded latency and intermittent 503s during scheduled marketing burst. Root cause tied to a cascade of KV cache evictions + autoscaler race leading to GPU OOM and traffic routed to lower-tier model variant. Immediate mitigations applied: temporary capacity reservation, tweak to autoscaler thresholds, manual routing rule. Longer-term actions: autoscaler guardrails, improved monitoring/alerting, runbook updates, canary policy improvements.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-28
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Priya Nair (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood CSM), Lena Ortiz (Aurora SRE), Marcus Bell (Aurora VP Eng), Diane Park (Aurora CTO), Tom Reyes (Aurora Platform)

Topics noted: postmortem follow-up, mitigations applied, long-term reliability work, runbook and testing plan, security/compliance questions

[00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is the postmortem follow-up for the 21st. We want to run through the timeline, confirm mitigations that we applied, and align on next steps. I'll hand over to Ethan to walk the technical timeline.

[00:28] Ethan: Yeah thanks. So quick tl;dr: during the marketing burst we saw a sharp increase in short-lived sessions which caused our prefix/KV cache to thrash, this led to a lot of cache misses and higher memory pressure on the inference nodes. At the same time the K8s autoscaler hit a race where scale-ups were delayed, a couple of pods hit GPU OOMs, and requests got routed to our fallback model variant which can't handle the concurrency so you saw 503s and increased tail latency.

[01:05] Lena: Sorry can I interrupt — when you say fallback model variant, is that the quantized small model you mentioned earlier or something else? We saw different error signatures in the logs.

[01:14] Ethan: Good question. It's the lower-capacity quantized variant — we sometimes call it 'rwd-lite' in internal notes; in the transcript of the incident it shows up as 'red-wd light' so apologies for inconsistent naming. That variant has reduced batch size limits and less KV cache allocation which amplified the problem.

[01:42] Marcus: So timeline wise, how long between the first cache eviction and when the fallback routing happened? We need to correlate with our dashboard spikes.

[01:50] Ethan: On our side it's about a 3 minute window from the first sustained cache miss spike to the first 503s. The autoscaler started reacting at minute 2 but the new pods weren't ready; then at minute 3 two pods hit OOM and were restarted which triggered the routing policy to divert traffic to lower tier to preserve availability.

[02:20] Diane: Is the root cause then more of a config/tuning problem, or is there an underlying bug in the autoscaler or cache management?

[02:27] Ethan: It's a mix. Primarily config/tuning — the autoscaler thresholds didn't account for very short lived high-QPS bursts that increase working set for the KV cache. There's also an optimization gap where eviction policy favours keeping some metadata over large prefixes; we have an engineering task to tighten that up. No single kernel-level bug was identified, but we will harden eviction heuristics.

[02:58] Lena: During the incident we also noticed a spike in IO on the node — could that have contributed to the delay in pod readiness?

[03:06] Ethan: Yes, startup involves loading quantized weights which touches NVMe; if nodes are saturated it slows readiness. One of our mitigations was to pre-warm nodes and keep a small buffer of warm pods, which we pushed during the incident.

[03:28] Priya: To be explicit about the immediate mitigations we put in place on the 21st: (1) temporary reserved capacity on your Dedicated pool for the next 72 hours, (2) adjusted autoscaler thresholds to be more aggressive on pod add, (3) manual routing override to prefer higher-capacity pool for critical routes, (4) pre-warm script to keep two spare warm pods per AZ. We communicated those in the ticket but wanted to confirm they're acceptable long-term or if you want different actions.

[04:05] Marcus: The temporary reserved capacity helped, yes. Cost will be our only hesitation long-term — we need more predictable scaling rather than always reserving capacity.

[04:14] Jordan: Totally, and that's in line with what we discussed — the goal is to avoid reserving big chunks. The plan is to implement autoscaler guardrails and better early-warning metrics so the system autos-scales before OOMs happen, that reduces the need for always-on reserved capacity.

[04:35] Lena: What alerts should we expect to see? Right now some of our alerts are high-level 5xx counts, which by the time they trigger it's already a problem.

[04:44] Ethan: We'll add two new metrics + alerts: sustained KV cache miss rate > X for Y seconds, and node startup latency above expected threshold. We also recommend an early-warning alert on pending pods in the cluster (pending for > 30s) and a high tail latency on the model enqueue time. We'll provide a concrete alert rule set.

[05:15] Tom: Could we get those as Prometheus rules? We'll push them to our existing alerting pipeline.

[05:20] Ethan: Yes, we'll export sample Prometheus rules and a Grafana dashboard.

[05:28] Diane: On security/compliance — you mentioned we shared some logs in the ticket. Can you confirm those are scrubbed and what retention policy Redwood keeps?

[05:38] Priya: Yes — logs shared to your org ticket were scrubbed for PII. As a reminder, our Hosted logs retention defaults to 30 days unless you have a Dedicated/Private agreement. For Dedicated deployments we can align retention with your policies and KMS settings. We'll attach the security artifacts and SOC2 section.

[06:02] Marcus: Good. Also, for the longer-term reliability work, what are the engineering deliverables and rough estimates?

[06:12] Ethan: Short list: 1) Autoscaler improvements — guardrails + faster scale up path (~3 sprints), 2) Eviction policy improvements for KV cache (~2 sprints), 3) Pre-warm and warm-pool features as configurable settings (~1-2 sprints), 4) Routing policy enhancements for smarter fallbacks (~2 sprints). We can break these into milestones and we'll propose an order based on biggest impact first (autoscaler and eviction policy).

[06:50] Lena: Can we get a prioritized timeline? We need to plan our release windows accordingly.

[06:56] Priya: We'll send a proposed timeline in the deck. Our recommendation is to prioritize: autoscaler guardrails first, then eviction heuristics, then warm-pool config, then routing improvements. We'll include a recommended canary plan for each change.

[07:18] Marcus: For canaries, will you support canary by customer? We want to test with a small percentage of traffic only on our routes first.

[07:27] Ethan: Yes, we support per-route canaries and can do a staged increase. We'll provide the rollout playbook.

[07:34] Diane: Any residual risk while you implement these? For example, could a future burst still hit us before autoscaler changes are in?

[07:44] Ethan: There is residual risk until autoscaler improvements are deployed. To mitigate in the interim: keep a small warm buffer (what we deployed), set the early-warning alerts, and we can keep a small reserved buffer during high-risk windows (marketing campaigns) — only when needed.

[08:01] Lena: Ok that sounds reasonable. One more question — in the postmortem you mentioned tenant isolation improvements for KV caches. Can you expand?

[08:11] Ethan: Right now the cache is shared with soft prioritization; we plan to add stronger per-customer partitioning of the KV cache so one tenant's working set won't evict others as easily. That's a medium effort but high impact for multi-tenant hosts.

[08:34] Marcus: That would be ideal. Also, I'd like to see the incident trace — the span traces you captured — can you attach them?

[08:41] Priya: We'll attach the tracing spans and the full timeline in the deck. We already added a short summary to the ticket.

[08:50] [pause, typing noises]

[09:02] Jordan: Quick ops note — we'll update our runbook template to include the new alerts + playbook steps: when to reserve capacity, who to escalate to, and the exact commands for manual routing override. I'll send the updated template.

[09:20] Lena: Thanks. For the synthetic load run, what's the recommended setup to reproduce? We tried replaying headers and saw different patterns.

[09:30] Ethan: We'll provide a replay script and a harness that simulates your real traffic mix (short session spikes and longer contexts). Recommendation is two runs: 75% of peak for pre-check, then 100% peak as scheduled. Record all node metrics and the model enqueue times.

[09:58] Marcus: Great. If the synthetic run still shows issues after your recommended config, what's the escalation path?

[10:07] Priya: Escalate to the SE on-call (Ethan) and we'll create a joint incident with our Engs. Jordan will coordinate. We'll also open a dedicated engineering ticket for collaboration.

[10:20] Diane: Sounds good. Any commercial implications we should discuss? If we ask for reserved capacity during marketing windows, it will change billing.

[10:29] Priya: We can work with finance on a burst plan — a temporary reserved-burst contract or credits — we'll include a pricing note in the follow-up.

[10:38] Marcus: Alright.

[10:40] Priya: To recap next steps quickly: I will share the postmortem deck and artifacts; Ethan will share autoscaler metrics, Prometheus rules, and the replay harness; Jordan will update the runbook and schedule the 2-week follow-up. Aurora will run the synthetic tests and share logs. Action items and due dates are in the ticket. Anything else?

[11:05] Diane: No, thanks. Appreciate the quick response on this.

[11:12] Lena: Thanks everyone.

[11:15] Priya: Thanks; we'll follow up via ticket and I'll send calendar invite for the follow-up.

[11:20] [meeting ends]

References / shared artifacts: postmortem slide deck (link in ticket), mitigation config (sample HPA manifests and warm-pool script), replay harness (link), security artifacts (SOC2, logging policy)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mislabels and minor transcription errors (product names like 'red-wd light' for rwd-lite).
